name: Terminal Velocity
statement: A falling body speeds up only until drag matches gravity, then falls at a steady maximum speed.
statementAccent: until drag matches gravity, then falls at a steady maximum speed
meaning: Terminal velocity is the maximum, constant speed that an object reaches as it falls through a fluid, usually air, when the downward force of gravity is exactly balanced by the upward resistive force of drag. As an object begins to fall it accelerates, but the drag it experiences grows as it speeds up, and eventually the drag equals the object's weight. At that point the net force on the object is zero, so it stops accelerating and continues to fall at a steady speed, its terminal velocity. The value depends on the object's weight, its size and shape, and the density of the fluid: a compact, heavy, or streamlined object has a high terminal velocity, while a light object with a large area, like a parachute or a feather, has a low one. Terminal velocity is a basic concept in the physics of falling bodies, explaining why a skydiver, a raindrop, and a dust mote each settle to their own steady descent speed rather than accelerating without limit.
mechanism: A falling object is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by drag, the resistance of the fluid it moves through. At the start, when the object is moving slowly, drag is small and gravity dominates, so the object accelerates. But drag increases with speed, and in the common high-speed regime it grows roughly with the square of the velocity, so as the object speeds up the retarding force climbs quickly. When the drag force grows to equal the object's weight, the two forces cancel, the net force becomes zero, and by Newton's laws the acceleration stops; the object then falls at a constant terminal velocity. The size of that speed follows from setting drag equal to weight, giving a terminal velocity that increases with the object's mass and decreases with its cross-sectional area, its drag coefficient (a measure of shape), and the fluid's density. This is why a parachute, by greatly increasing area, drastically lowers terminal velocity, and why a streamlined, dense object falls fast. A skydiver in a spread, belly-to-earth posture reaches roughly two hundred kilometres per hour.

examples.text: A skydiver spread belly-to-earth reaches a terminal velocity of roughly two hundred kilometres per hour, faster head-down and slower with a parachute.
Opening a parachute hugely increases area and drag, lowering terminal velocity to a speed safe for landing.
Small raindrops have low terminal velocities, which is why rain falls gently rather than striking with the force of an unchecked fall.

variants.name: The drag balance
variants.text: The condition defining terminal velocity, where the upward drag force exactly equals the object's weight so net force is zero.

variants.name: Shape and area dependence
variants.text: The way terminal velocity falls with larger cross-sectional area and drag coefficient, as a parachute demonstrates, and rises with mass.

whyItMatters: Terminal velocity is a fundamental idea in the physics of motion through a fluid, explaining why falling objects do not accelerate without limit but settle to a steady speed set by the balance of gravity and drag. It is essential to understanding skydiving and parachuting, where controlling body position and deploying a canopy change the terminal velocity between a fast free fall and a safe landing speed, and it is central to the design of parachutes, drag chutes, and safety equipment. In nature it governs how fast rain, hail, snow, seeds, spores, and dust fall, shaping weather, erosion, and the dispersal of life, and it explains why small creatures can survive falls that would injure larger ones. In engineering and science it informs sedimentation, aerosol behaviour, and the fall of particles through fluids. As the clear resolution of the competition between gravity and air resistance, terminal velocity connects Newton's laws to a wide range of everyday and technical phenomena of falling.

working.text: let gravity accelerate the object downward, with drag initially small at low speed.
as speed rises, let drag increase, roughly with the square of velocity, until it approaches the object's weight.
when drag equals weight the net force is zero, so acceleration stops and the object falls at constant terminal velocity.

limits: Terminal velocity depends on the object's weight, size, shape, and the fluid's density, so it is not a single universal number; the skydiver's roughly two hundred kilometres per hour applies to a spread posture at ordinary altitude and varies with body position, and record free-fall speeds far higher are achieved in the thin air of very high altitude. The simple square-law drag treatment applies to the high-speed turbulent regime; very small or slow objects fall in a different regime where drag is proportional to speed. Terminal velocity assumes the object has fallen far enough to reach the balance, and it changes if conditions change, such as air density with altitude or a parachute opening. So terminal velocity robustly describes the steady fall speed set by drag balancing weight, with its value depending on the specific object, posture, and fluid conditions.
misreadings: Terminal velocity is not the speed at which an object stops falling; it is the constant speed at which it keeps falling once drag balances gravity. It is not the same for all objects, since it depends on weight, area, shape, and fluid density, which is why a parachute falls slowly and a stone fast. And it is not a fixed number for a skydiver, varying with body position and air density, so treating terminal velocity as a halt, or as one universal value, misreads a steady descent speed set by the balance between an object's weight and the drag it meets.
origin: A basic concept in the physics of falling bodies through a fluid: the steady maximum speed reached when drag balances gravity, dependent on weight, shape, area, and fluid density.
